---
title: "Part 1 — The command line"
subtitle: "Terminal, paths, commands, pipes and wildcards"
---

You need this part before your first practical. At the end of it, you can open
a terminal, say where you are, move around, read a command and its parameters,
and send the output of one command into another.

Work through it at a terminal, and type the commands as you go. It takes about
an evening.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Every command on this page is tested

Each time this site is built, the `bash` blocks below run on a clean Linux
machine. If a command is on this page, it ran without an error. Your machine can
still have other versions or other defaults, but the example contains no typo.
:::

# Opening a terminal

A **terminal** (dt. *Terminal*) is a window that lets you type commands. The
program that reads what you type and runs it is the **shell** (dt. *Kommando­zeile*
or *Shell*). On almost every computer you will use, the shell is `bash`, or
`zsh`, which is very similar.

::: {.callout-important}
## This material targets Linux

In particular, it targets **Ubuntu**, the Linux you are most likely to use.
Everything here is written and tested on Ubuntu.

WSL2 on Windows is Linux, so it is covered too. macOS is similar but not the
same. This page notes the differences where they are important, but it cannot
cover a Mac completely.
:::

**Linux** — search the applications menu for *Terminal*. On Ubuntu,
<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Alt</kbd>+<kbd>T</kbd> opens one directly. The rest of this
page assumes Linux.

**Windows** — you need **WSL2** (Windows Subsystem for Linux). It runs a real
Ubuntu inside Windows. This is not a second-best solution: much scientific
software is not available for Windows at all, so on Windows the answer is to run
Linux. Open PowerShell as administrator and type:

```powershell
wsl --install
```

Restart the computer and wait until the setup is complete. Choose a username
and a password. After that, start *Ubuntu* from the Start menu. Everything below
then works for you as written, because you are now running Linux.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do this before the practical, not during it

The WSL2 installation needs a restart and a download. Sometimes you must also
switch on virtualisation in the BIOS. Solve this at home when you have time, not
in the first ten minutes of a practical session.
:::

**macOS** — *Terminal* is in `Applications → Utilities`. Spotlight
(<kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>Space</kbd>, then type "terminal") is quicker. macOS is based
on Unix, so all the concepts are the same and most commands work without change.

::: {.callout-note}
## If you are on a Mac, expect some things to differ

Linux comes with the **GNU** versions of the basic tools. macOS comes with the
older **BSD** versions. They agree on the important things and differ in
details. The most visible difference: BSD tools usually do **not** accept
`--help` or long parameter names such as `--lines`. They accept only the short
form, such as `-n`.

This page uses the form that works on both wherever it can. Outside this page,
a Mac will sometimes not follow the instructions. The usual message is
`unrecognized option`, and the usual fix is to use the short parameter. This
material cannot cover every platform, and Linux is the one it covers.
:::

**No installation at all** — if you only want to try the commands on this page
first, [webvm.io](https://webvm.io) starts a real Debian Linux in a browser tab.
You install nothing and need no account. It is enough for everything in Part 1.

::: {.callout-note}
## What the browser one is not

It forgets everything when you close the tab, and you cannot install software
in it. So from Part 2 on, you need one of the other ways above. Use it to start
today, not as your working computer.
:::

## What you are looking at

You will see something like this.

![The prompt, and what each part of it tells you.](../figures/prompt-anatomy.svg){#fig-prompt
fig-alt="A terminal window showing the prompt: user1, an at sign, machine, a
colon, tilde slash projects, then a dollar sign and a block cursor. A key
identifies user1 as your username, machine as the computer you are on, tilde
slash projects as where you are right now, and the dollar sign as the shell
being ready and waiting."}

This is the **prompt**: it shows that the shell is ready. The most important
part is **where you are now**. It changes as you move around. Beginners are most
often confused about where they are, and the prompt answers this question.

The `$` marks the end of the prompt. You never type it.

On this page, code blocks show the command *without* a prompt, so you can copy
them cleanly. Where output is shown, it is in a separate block.

::: {.callout-important}
## Pasting into a terminal takes an extra key

<kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> will not paste here.

| | |
|---|---|
| paste *into* the terminal | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> |
| copy *from* the terminal | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> |

Here is the reason. In a terminal, <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> already means
**stop the command that is running** (see *Getting unstuck* at the end of this
page). This meaning is much older than copy and paste. If you press it to copy,
you stop the command that you were waiting for.

On a Mac, the normal <kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> and <kbd>⌘</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd>
work, so this problem does not occur.
:::

# Where am I?

Beginners are most often confused because they do not know where they are. The
shell is always *in* one directory. Most commands work on that directory, unless
you tell them otherwise.

`pwd` — **p**rint **w**orking **d**irectory — shows where you are:

```bash
pwd
```

```text
/home/user
```

`ls` — **l**i**s**t — shows what is in the current directory:

```bash
ls
```

If nothing is printed, the directory is empty. This is a real answer, not an
error. You will get used to this: **most commands print nothing when they
work**. They print a message only when something goes wrong.

`ls` takes parameters that change what it shows:

```bash
ls -l
ls -a
ls -lh
```

- `-l` — **l**ong format: one file per line, with size, date and permissions.
- `-a` — **a**ll, including hidden files (those whose names start with a dot).
- `-lh` — long format with **h**uman-readable sizes (`4.0K` rather than `4096`).

The last one combines two parameters in one word. This is normal: `-lh` means
the same as `-l -h`.

### Reading `ls -l` output

A long listing shows six things on one line:

```text
-rw-r--r--  1  user1  staff  1048576  Sep 26 07:08  data.csv
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `-rw-r--r--` | who may read, write and run it. A leading `d` here means it is a **d**irectory. |
| `1` | number of links — ignore it for now |
| `user1` | the owner |
| `staff` | the owner's group |
| `1048576` | size in bytes (`-h` turns this into `1.0M`) |
| `Sep 26 07:08` | when it was last changed |

You do not need to read the permissions yet. But remember that this column
exists: when you see `Permission denied` later, this column is the reason.

::: {.callout-important}
## Everything is case-sensitive

`Data.csv`, `data.csv` and `DATA.CSV` are three different files, and `LS` is not
a command. Windows does not work this way, so this is a very common mistake. The
error message (`No such file or directory`) does not mention upper and lower
case. So it looks as if the file is missing, but the file is there.
:::

## The filesystem is one tree

Everything on the computer is inside a **single** directory called the
**root**, written `/`. There are no drive letters — no `C:`, no `D:`. A USB
stick, a second hard disk and a network drive all appear as directories
*somewhere inside this one tree*.

This is the biggest difference from Windows. Look at the tree first, because
paths only make sense with it.

![The filesystem is a single tree with `/` at its root. Directories branch;
files are leaves. Your own files live under `/home/<your name>/`.](../figures/filesystem-tree.svg){#fig-tree
fig-alt="A tree diagram. A single root node labelled forward-slash branches into
three directories: home, bin and etc. home branches into user1, user2 and user3.
user1 branches into Documents and Downloads, plus three files: notes.md,
data.csv and myscript.sh. bin contains three programs: ls, mkdir and bash."}

You will use two parts of this tree immediately:

- **`/home/<your name>/`** — your own files. You start here, and almost all your
  work belongs here. Its short form is `~`.
- **`/bin`, `/usr/bin`** — the programs. `ls` is a file on the disk, and it is
  here. So a command is a program in a directory. This is why "command not
  found" means that the shell cannot find a *file*.

## Directories and paths

A **path** (dt. *Pfad*) is the address of a file or directory: a route through
the tree. There are two kinds of path. The difference between them is the most
important point in this section.

An **absolute path** starts at the root, `/`. So it means the same thing, no
matter where you are. Compare it with @fig-tree: it is the route from `/` down
to the file:

```text
/home/user1/data.csv
```

A **relative path** starts from where you are now. If you are in
`/home/user1`, the path to the same file is only:

```text
data.csv
```

The relative path is shorter, and you will type it most of the time. It is
also why `pwd` is important: the same relative path means different things,
depending on where you are.

You will see three short forms all the time:

| | |
|---|---|
| `.` | the current directory |
| `..` | the directory one level up |
| `~` | your home directory |

So `~/projects` is the `projects` folder in your home directory, wherever that
is. And `../results` is a `results` folder next to the one you are in.

## Moving around

`cd` — **c**hange **d**irectory:

```bash
cd /tmp
pwd
```

```text
/tmp
```

Some useful forms:

```bash
cd ~
cd ..
cd -
```

- `cd ~` — go to your home directory. `cd` alone does the same.
- `cd ..` — go up one level.
- `cd -` — go back to the directory you were in before. This is often useful.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Press Tab. Always.

Type the first few letters of a name and press <kbd>Tab</kbd>. The shell
completes the name. If nothing happens, press <kbd>Tab</kbd> twice to see the
possible names.

This is more than a small help. It prevents almost all typos, and it shows you
that the file or directory exists. People who use Tab find the terminal much
easier than people who do not. Use it from your first day.
:::

# Making, copying and removing

First, make a place to work. These commands create a small directory tree. The
rest of this page uses it.

```bash
mkdir -p practice/data
cd practice
ls
```

```text
data
```

`mkdir` **m**a**k**es a **dir**ectory. The `-p` parameter means "also make the
parent directories if necessary, and give no error if the directory already
exists". This is why one command can create both `practice` and `practice/data`.

`echo` prints its argument. On its own, this looks useless:

```bash
echo "hello"
```

```text
hello
```

But the next examples send this output into a file instead of to the screen.
This is the fastest way to write text into a file without an editor. The section
*Redirection and pipes* below explains how this works. For now, read
`echo "text" > file` as "write text into file".

Now create some files to practise with:

```bash
echo "alpha" > data/first.txt
echo "beta" > data/second.txt
ls data
```

```text
first.txt
second.txt
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it now

You now have two real files to practise with. Type `cat data/fi` and press
<kbd>Tab</kbd>. The shell completes it to `data/first.txt`. This is the Tab
habit from above, used on a real file.
:::

Copying, renaming and moving:

```bash
cp data/first.txt data/copy.txt
mv data/copy.txt data/renamed.txt
ls data
```

```text
first.txt
renamed.txt
second.txt
```

`cp` copies, and `mv` moves. To rename a file, you also use `mv`: you move it
from one name to another name in the same directory. There is no separate
command for renaming.

## Deleting, and why it is different

```bash
rm data/renamed.txt
ls data
```

```text
first.txt
second.txt
```

::: {.callout-important}
## There is no recycle bin

`rm` does not move a file to a trash folder. It deletes the file. You cannot
undo it, and no window asks whether you are sure.

Learn these three habits now:

- **`ls` first, `rm` second.** Run `ls` with the same names that you want to
  delete. If `ls` shows what you expect, `rm` deletes what you expect.
- **Type the name with Tab, not from memory.** If the shell completed a name,
  the file exists and the name is spelled correctly. A name typed from memory
  is a guess, and a typo in an `rm` command can delete the wrong file.
- **Be very careful with `rm -r`.** It deletes a directory and everything inside
  it. Together with a wildcard or an extra space, it can delete a whole day's
  work.
:::

# Commands and parameters

Almost every command has the same structure:

```text
command  -parameters  arguments
```

- the **command** — the program that you run.
- **parameters**, also called flags or options — they change *how* the program
  works.
- **arguments** — usually what the program should work *on*, for example a
  file name.

There are two styles of parameters, and most tools accept both:

| style | looks like | notes |
|---|---|---|
| **short** | `-l`, `-h`, `-n 5` | one letter; several can be combined as `-lh` |
| **long** | `--long`, `--lines 5` | two dashes, a whole word, easier to read later |

Short parameters work everywhere. Long parameters are a GNU convention, so they
work on Linux but often not on macOS (see the note at the top of this page).

Some parameters need a value, and some do not:

```bash
head -n 1 data/first.txt
```

```text
alpha
```

Here `-n` takes the value `1`, and `data/first.txt` is the argument.

## Spaces split arguments — so avoid them in names

This follows from what an argument is. The shell splits what you type at each
space, *before* the command receives it. So the shell cannot tell a space
inside a file name from a space between two arguments.

```bash
mkdir -p "lab notebook"
ls
```

```text
lab notebook
```

This worked because of the quotes. Without the quotes:

```{.bash .no-run}
cd lab notebook
```

```text
bash: cd: lab: No such file or directory
```

`cd` receives **two** arguments, `lab` and `notebook`, not one. It looks for a
directory with the name `lab`, which does not exist. Quotes fix this:

```bash
cd "lab notebook"
pwd
cd ..
```

But you must remember the quotes **every time**, in every command. The real
fix is simpler: **do not create files or folders with spaces in their names.**
Use `lab_notebook` or `lab-notebook` instead, and the problem never occurs.

This problem is real. It is the most common way in which a beginner's own files
cause errors in the terminal. Graphical file managers and Windows allow spaces
in names, so beginners meet the problem for the first time in the terminal.

::: {.callout-tip}
Tab completion also protects you here. If you complete a name that contains a
space, the shell adds the quotes or the escape characters for you. This is one
more reason to use Tab, even when you think you remember the name.
:::

## A realistic invocation

A real command usually has more than one parameter. Here is an example with
`sort`, an ordinary tool. The command sorts a table by its second column, as
numbers, with the largest number first.

```bash
printf "alpha,12\nbeta,7\ngamma,103\n" > scores.csv
sort -t, -k2 -n -r scores.csv
```

```text
gamma,103
alpha,12
beta,7
```

There are four parameters, and each one does one thing:

| | |
|---|---|
| `-t,` | the columns are separated by commas |
| `-k2` | sort on column 2 |
| `-n` | compare as **n**umbers, not text |
| `-r` | **r**everse, so largest first |

Without `-n`, `103` comes before `12`, because as *text* it starts with a `1`
followed by a `0`. This is not a bug. The command did what you asked for, not
what you meant. Parameters exist to make this difference clear.

Scientific tools often have more parameters, and they often mix the two styles:

```{.bash .no-run}
some_tool --input data/ --output results/ -t 4 --verbose
```

You can read this command without knowing the tool. `--input` and `--output`
say where the data comes from and where the results go. `-t 4` almost always
means "use 4 threads". `--verbose` tells the tool to print more information
about what it does. **Read an unknown command by its parameters.** The
structure is almost always the same, whatever the tool does.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Prefer long parameters in anything you keep

On Linux, `-n 1` and `--lines 1` do the same thing. Short parameters are
quicker to type. Long parameters are much easier to read six months later, and
in the methods section of a report they explain themselves. So type the short
form at the terminal, and use the long form in anything you save. But remember
that a script with long parameters does not run on a Mac.
:::

## Long commands and the backslash

Real commands can be so long that they are written on several lines. A
backslash at the end of a line means **"this command continues on the next
line"**:

```bash
head \
  -n 1 \
  data/second.txt
```

```text
beta
```

This is the same command as `head -n 1 data/second.txt`. The backslashes are
only there to make it easier for people to read.

::: {.callout-warning}
## The backslash must be the last character on the line

Not a space, not a comment: the backslash must be the very last character. If
there is a space after the backslash, the command does not continue. The error
message then points to the *next* line, which is confusing.

This small detail is important. In a typical practical, almost a quarter of the
commands are written on several lines in this way. A student who cannot read
the backslash cannot copy most of the session correctly.
:::

## Finding out what a command does

Try these three things, in this order:

```{.bash .no-run}
head --help
```

On Linux, most commands accept `--help` and print a short summary. This is the
fastest answer, and it is usually enough. On macOS, the basic tools are the BSD
versions, and most of them do not accept `--help`. On a Mac, use `man`
directly.

```{.bash .no-run}
man head
```

`man` — **man**ual — opens the full documentation in a pager. Scroll with the
arrow keys or <kbd>Space</kbd>, search by typing `/word`, and **quit with `q`**.
Many beginners get stuck here because they do not know that `q` quits.

Many tools print a short usage text if you run them without arguments. A few
tools wait for input instead. Then <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> stops them.

# Looking at files

You rarely want to print a whole file. These four commands cover almost every
case:

```bash
cat data/first.txt
```

```text
alpha
```

`cat` prints the whole file. This is fine for a short file, but a mistake for
a large one: printing a million lines takes time and tells you nothing.

```bash
head -n 2 data/first.txt
tail -n 1 data/second.txt
```

```text
alpha
beta
```

`head` shows the first lines, and `tail` the last lines. Both show 10 lines if
you do not say otherwise.

```bash
wc -l data/first.txt
```

```text
1 data/first.txt
```

`wc` counts words (**w**ord **c**ount), and `-l` makes it count **l**ines
instead. Counting lines is by far the most common use.

To read a large file page by page, use `less`. It opens the file in the same
pager that `man` uses:

```{.bash .no-run}
less data/first.txt
```

The keys are the same: arrows and <kbd>Space</kbd> to move, `/word` to search,
`q` to quit.

## Editing files: use VS Code

Sooner or later you need to *change* a file, not only look at it. There are
editors that run in the terminal: `nano` is the easy one, and `vim` is the
difficult one. You will meet them some day, especially on a server where no
other editor is available.

**For everything else, use [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com).**
This is a strong recommendation, for these reasons:

- It edits files and gives you a **terminal in the same window**. You do not
  have to switch between the file and the command that reads it.
- It knows the formats you will use — Markdown, JSON, CSV, YAML, Python. Its
  syntax highlighting shows you when a file contains an error.
- With its **WSL** extension, Windows users can edit Linux files directly,
  without copying them. On Windows, this is almost necessary.
- It is free, and many people in the field use it, so it is easy to find
  help.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do not edit these files in Word

A word processor adds formatting, curly quotes and its own line endings, and it
does not tell you. The file looks correct on the screen, but programs cannot
read it, and the error message does not say why. Use a text editor for text
files.
:::

# Redirection and pipes

This section is the main reason to learn the command line. Graphical programs
have nothing like it.

## Three streams, not one

Every command has three channels. If you know them, several things that look
like bugs make sense:

| stream | | |
|---|---|---|
| **stdin** | standard input | what goes *in* — usually what you type, or another command's output |
| **stdout** | standard output | the actual result |
| **stderr** | standard error | warnings and error messages |

The important consequence: **`>` and `|` move only stdout.** Errors and
warnings still go to the screen. So if you send the output of a command to a
file and still see red text, nothing is broken: the red text is stderr. This is
intended. It means that an error message never ends up inside your results file
without you seeing it.

## Sending output to a file

Normally a command prints its result on the screen. `>` sends the result to a
file instead:

```bash
head -n 1 data/first.txt > result.txt
cat result.txt
```

```text
alpha
```

::: {.callout-warning}
`>` **overwrites** the file without a warning. `>>` adds to the end of the file
instead. This is how people empty a file by accident.
:::

```bash
echo "second line" >> result.txt
cat result.txt
```

```text
alpha
second line
```

## Sending output to another command

`|` — the **pipe** (dt. *Pipe* or *Rohr*) — takes the output of one command and
gives it to the next command as input. No file is written.

First, create a file to filter:

```bash
printf "banana\napple\ncherry\napple\n" > fruit.txt
cat fruit.txt
```

```text
banana
apple
cherry
apple
```

Now connect several commands:

```bash
sort fruit.txt | uniq -c | sort -rn
```

```text
      2 apple
      1 cherry
      1 banana
```

Read it from left to right: sort the lines, then count how often each line
occurs, then sort this result as numbers (`-n`) in reverse order (`-r`).
`uniq -c` needs sorted input, and this is why `sort` comes first.

`grep` finds the lines that match a pattern. It is probably the most useful
command on this page:

```bash
grep "an" fruit.txt
```

```text
banana
```

Now combine the two ideas: filter, then save:

```bash
grep "ap" fruit.txt | sort > apples.txt
cat apples.txt
```

```text
apple
apple
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## This is the whole idea

Each of these commands does one small thing, and none of them knows about the
others. With the pipe, a few simple tools can answer a question that no single
program was written for.

When you see a long command in a practical, read it as a sentence, with `|`
between the parts. It almost always says: *take this, keep the interesting
part, count it, sort it.*
:::

# Wildcards

With a **wildcard** (dt. *Platzhalter*), one name can refer to many files. The
shell replaces the wildcard with the matching file names *before* the command
runs. So the command itself never sees the `*`.

```bash
ls data/*.txt
```

```text
data/first.txt
data/second.txt
```

| | |
|---|---|
| `*` | any number of characters, including none |
| `?` | exactly one character |
| `[abc]` | any one of the listed characters |

```bash
ls data/?econd.txt
```

```text
data/second.txt
```

The most common use is to run one command on a whole set of files:

```bash
wc -l data/*.txt
```

```text
1 data/first.txt
1 data/second.txt
2 total
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Check a wildcard with `ls` before using it with anything destructive

`ls` and `rm` expand `*` in the same way. So `ls` shows you which files `rm`
would delete, without any risk. This is the same habit as above, and this is
why we repeat it here.
:::

# Variables, briefly

You will read variables before you write any: in other people's instructions,
or in the output of an installer. This section explains enough to recognise
them:

```bash
FOOBAR="hello world"
echo $FOOBAR
```

```text
hello world
```

To set a variable, write `NAME=value`, with **no spaces around the `=`**.
`FOOBAR = "hi"` does not set a variable: the shell tries to run a command called
`FOOBAR`, which almost certainly does not exist. To read the value of a
variable, put a `$` in front of its name: `$FOOBAR`, not `FOOBAR`.

You have already used two variables without knowing their names. `$HOME` is
your home directory (`~` is its short form). `$PATH` is the list of directories
in which the shell looks for the program file of a command. This is *why*
"command not found" is a real error: the shell looked in every directory on
this list and did not find the program. Both variables are already set, so you
do not need to define them.

```bash
echo $HOME
```

This is all that this page covers about variables. Writing your own scripts
with variables, loops and conditions is programming, and it belongs in a
programming course.

# Getting unstuck

This short list will save you more time than anything else on this page.

| situation | what to do |
|---|---|
| A command is running and you want it to stop | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> |
| You are stuck in a pager (`man`, `less`) | `q` |
| The prompt has vanished and nothing responds | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>, then <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>D</kbd> |
| You want the command you ran a minute ago | <kbd>↑</kbd> arrow, repeatedly |
| You want one you ran yesterday | `history`, or <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>R</kbd> and start typing |
| The screen is a mess | `clear` |
| You typed a long command and want to fix the start | <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>A</kbd> jumps to the beginning |
| You are not sure a name is spelled right | Do not guess — press <kbd>Tab</kbd> |
| You pressed <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to copy, and the command stopped | That is what it means here. Copy is <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd>, paste <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>V</kbd> |

## Reading an error message

Error messages look unfriendly, but they usually say something simple. These
are the three you will meet first:

```text
bash: sortt: command not found
```

The shell cannot find this program. Usually this is a typo. Sometimes the tool
is not installed yet: Part 2 explains how to install tools.

```text
ls: cannot access 'dta': No such file or directory
```

The path is wrong. Run `pwd`, then `ls` to see what is really there. Almost
always, you are not in the directory that you think you are in.

```text
bash: result.txt: Permission denied
```

You do not have the permission to do this here. This often happens when you
are outside your home directory.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Read the last line first

If a command fails and prints twenty lines, the useful line is usually the last
one or the first one, rarely one in the middle. Also, a command that prints a
warning has not necessarily failed. Warnings and errors are different, and many
tools print warnings every time they run.
:::

# What you should be able to do now

Check yourself against this list. If you can do everything on it, you are
ready for a first practical.

- [ ] Open a terminal, by whichever route works for you — on Windows that means
      WSL2, unless you are using the browser one.
- [ ] Say where you are (`pwd`) and what is there (`ls`).
- [ ] Move around with `cd`, including `..` and `~`.
- [ ] Explain why there is no `C:` drive, and what `/` is.
- [ ] Tell an absolute path from a relative one, and explain why it matters.
- [ ] Have VS Code installed, and on Windows its WSL extension.
- [ ] Make a directory, copy, rename and delete a file — carefully.
- [ ] Read a command and name its parameters and arguments.
- [ ] Read a command written across several lines with backslashes.
- [ ] Explain why a space in a filename breaks a command, and avoid making one.
- [ ] Find out what a command does, with `--help` or `man`, and quit the pager.
- [ ] Send output to a file with `>`, and know what `>>` does differently.
- [ ] Chain two commands with a pipe and explain what each half does.
- [ ] Say why an error message still appears on screen when you redirect output.
- [ ] Use `*` to act on a set of files, having checked it with `ls` first.
- [ ] Read `NAME=value` and `$NAME`, and say what `$HOME` and `$PATH` are.
- [ ] Stop a running command, and get back a command you ran earlier.
- [ ] Use Tab to complete a name rather than typing it from memory.

Nothing in this list asks you to memorise commands. Everybody looks commands
up, all the time. What matters is that you know what is possible, and what to
search for.
